intro: Au bord d’une source is the fourth piece of Liszt’s Années de pèlerinage I: Suisse, S. 160; in it the left hand crosses over the right to play short notes above the running accompaniment. Eugen d’Albert, a pupil of Liszt, plays it on an early Odeon disc.

sections.label: A · Ripples and crossed hands
sections.mNote: Short notes dart above and below the right hand’s semiquavers.

sections.label: B · The spring in full flow
sections.mNote: Scales and arpeggios carry the tune across the keyboard.

sections.label: A′ · The ripples subside
sections.mNote: The flowing piano writing continues towards the close.

cues.title: Opening, crossed hands
cues.text: Liszt marks the opening Allegretto grazioso, with the melody sweet and tranquil. The right hand plays semiquavers. The left plays short notes, first beneath them, then two octaves higher.
cues.evidence: The opening notation and markings are reproduced on IMSLP’s work page: https://imslp.org/wiki/Années_de_pèlerinage_I,_S.160_(Liszt,_Franz). The crossed-hand pattern is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Au_bord_d%27une_source.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Switzerland with Marie d’Agoult, 1835
cues.text: In 1835 Liszt left Paris with Marie d’Agoult. They settled in Switzerland, where he taught at the Geneva Conservatory; their daughter Blandine was born in December. He later gathered his Swiss pieces, this one among them, into Années de pèlerinage.
cues.evidence: Liszt chronology, entries for 1835–36: https://www.liszt.org/p/chronology.html. The miniature’s earlier and revised versions are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Au_bord_d%27une_source.

cues.title: D’Albert, Glasgow to Weimar
cues.text: D’Albert was born in Glasgow and studied in London under Arthur Sullivan. While still a teenager he went to Vienna and stayed with the conductor Hans Richter. He then joined Liszt’s pupils in Weimar.
cues.evidence: Eliot Levin’s biography gives d’Albert’s Glasgow birth, London training, stay with Richter from late 1881 and subsequent study with Liszt: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/c.asp?c=C6.

cues.title: Scales and arpeggios between statements
cues.text: Scales and arpeggios connect the successive statements of the melody. They climb into the piano’s highest register, run down again and lead back into the tune.
cues.evidence: The account of the piano writing at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Au_bord_d%27une_source describes the connecting scales and arpeggios, their ascent and descent, and the return to the melody.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

composer.born: 22 October 1811, Doborján, Kingdom of Hungary (now Raiding, Austria)
composer.epithet: Pianist whose playing drew orchestral sound from the keyboard, and who at the end of his life turned to sparse music at the piano.
facts: Carl Czerny and Antonio Salieri in Vienna; Anton Reicha in Paris
Free masterclasses; founding president of the Budapest music academy, 1875
Piano works and transcriptions; thirteen symphonic poems; symphonies, concertos and sacred music
composer.background:
Writing from Albano in June 1839, Liszt told Princess Cristina Belgiojoso about the concerts he had been giving alone in Rome. No singer came on between his pieces, and no other soloist shared the bill. He played his transcription of the William Tell Overture, fantasies on opera tunes, studies and improvisations. Between numbers he talked to the audience. “The concert is me,” he joked.

His father Adam had begun the piano lessons in Doborján, a German-speaking village in the Kingdom of Hungary, where he worked on an Esterházy estate. Liszt always counted Hungary as his homeland, though the languages he used most easily were German and French. The family went to Vienna in 1822. Carl Czerny, a former pupil of Beethoven, taught him piano, and Antonio Salieri taught him composition. In 1823 the family moved to Paris, where the Conservatoire refused to admit a foreigner. He continued his education with private lessons, including work with Anton Reicha.
